source_refs.note: Book p. 37: 3.3 Absolute Value, the definition of |x| and the graph of y = |x| (printed before 3.3.1); the rules for |x| = a, |x| < a, |x| > a and all callouts marked Teaching note / Key points / Common mistake are ours.

blocks.text: The absolute value of \(x\), is defined as

blocks.text_alt: the absolute value of x equals x when x is greater than or equal to 0, and minus x when x is less than 0

blocks.alt: Graph of y = |x| on a grid, x from minus 4 to 4 and y up to 4: a V shape with its corner at the origin and two straight arms with arrowheads rising at 45 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure: the graph of y = |x| (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The absolute value of a number is its distance from 0 on the number line. A distance is never negative, so \(|x| \ge 0\) for every real \(x\).
Examples: \(|5| = 5\), \(|-5| = 5\), \(|0| = 0\).
Why "\(-x\)" for \(x < 0\)? If \(x\) is negative, then \(-x\) is positive. For \(x = -3\): \(|-3| = -(-3) = 3\). So the second line of the definition simply removes the minus sign.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Reading the graph: for \(x \ge 0\) the graph is the line \(y = x\); for \(x < 0\) it is the line \(y = -x\). Together they form a V with its corner at the origin. The graph is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis because \(|-x| = |x|\), and it never goes below the \(x\)-axis because \(|x| \ge 0\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Three rules that follow from the definition (for a number \(a > 0\)); 3.3.1 and 3.3.2 use them all the time:
\(|E| = a\) means \(E = a\) or \(E = -a\) (written \(E = \pm a\)).
\(|E| < a\) means \(-a < E < a\) (both at the same time: "and").
\(|E| > a\) means \(E < -a\) or \(E > a\) (one of the two: "or").
Here \(E\) can be any expression, for example \(x^{2} - 4\). The same holds with \(\le\) and \(\ge\).
On the number line: \(|E| < a\) is the part between \(-a\) and \(a\); \(|E| > a\) is the two parts outside.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(|x| = x\) for \(x \ge 0\) and \(|x| = -x\) for \(x < 0\).
2. \(|x|\) is the distance of \(x\) from 0, so \(|x| \ge 0\) and \(|-x| = |x|\).
3. The graph of \(y = |x|\) is a V with its corner at \((0, 0)\).
4. \(|E| = a \Leftrightarrow E = \pm a\); \(|E| < a \Leftrightarrow -a < E < a\); \(|E| > a \Leftrightarrow E < -a\) or \(E > a\) (\(a > 0\)).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Thinking \(|x| = -x\) is always negative: for \(x < 0\), \(-x\) is positive.
2. Writing \(|-a| = -a\) for a letter \(a\): this is true only when \(a \le 0\).
3. Using "or" for \(|E| < a\): it is "and", the values between \(-a\) and \(a\).
4. Solving \(|E| = a\) with \(a < 0\): there is no solution, because an absolute value is never negative.
